real_estate.homebuilder: The Fed raised its own rate forecast to 4.1% for this year, so the wait for cheaper money just got a longer timeline.
real_estate.commentary:
Rates barely moved to finish the week. Mortgage News Daily had the 30-year at 7.20% and the 15-year at 6.83% Friday, still a touch under Wednesday's one year high of 7.24%. The 10-Year Treasury closed at 5.01%, back to its own high for the year.

Here is what the Fed's September projections mean for you, in plain terms. The Fed does not set mortgage rates, but it sets the tone. In June the typical Fed official expected the Fed's rate to be 3.8% at the end of this year. Now they expect 4.1%, which is about one more quarter point increase, and they expect it to come down more slowly after that. The reason sits in the same table: they see inflation at 3.7% this year.

For a buyer that means the plan of waiting for rates to drop just got a longer timeline.

• The local math: at Fremont's median list price of $1,200,000, a 20% down loan is $960,000, under Alameda County's $1,249,125 high-balance conforming limit.
• At 7.20%, principal and interest run about $6,516 a month, and every eighth of a point is about $81.

📍 Alameda County (Fremont Focus)

• Board wide: 2,774 listings across our 15 city table, counting active and in contract together, with 189 coming soon and 239 brand new.
• Five city ledger: 717 live listings across Fremont, Hayward, Milpitas, Newark and Union City. 631 are already on the market and 86 are coming soon.
• Fremont: 255 live, 200 active, 37 coming soon, 18 brand new. The median on market list price is $1,200,000 at $789 a square foot, and the typical active listing has been out 29 days.
• The rest of the ledger: Hayward 186, Milpitas 116, Newark 91, Union City 69.
• Across all five cities the median is $1,099,000 at $680 a square foot. 282 homes are priced under a million, and 158 have been sitting 60 days or longer.

What this means for you: the ledger eased to 717 from 723, with Fremont down six and Union City up three. Homes sitting 60 days or longer have held at 158 for three days straight, which tells you the slow stuff is not moving, not that buyers left. Sellers: price to today's 7.2%, not to the rate you had in mind in June.

feature_images.caption: The Fed now expects its own rate to be higher at the end of this year than it did in June, and to come down more slowly after that.
feature_images.source: Source: Federal Reserve, Summary of Economic Projections, September 16, 2026, median projections.

economy.commentary:
The world had 65 active armed conflicts in 2025, the most since record keeping began in 1946, and 8 of them were one state fighting another, up from 2 in 2023. Thirteen counted as wars, the most since 1992.

This is not a foreign news item for a homeowner. It is an energy and shipping story with a price tag. Brent crude settled at $103.87 Friday and has spent this year above $100, which feeds fuel, freight and insurance costs into almost everything else. That is the same inflation the Fed says will run 3.7% this year, and the reason its rate path moved up instead of down. Conflict abroad, then higher costs, then a slower path to cheaper money here.

Gold and silver kept climbing on the same worry, with gold up 1.01% Friday to $4,424.90 and silver up 2.18% to $67.15.

One note on the chart. The widely shared version plots only the total. We added the state against state line from the same dataset, because that is the part that moves oil and shipping, and its 8 is a record too. Our early years also read lower than that version, because the research group revises its history with each release and we used one release throughout.

feature_images.alt: Line chart of active state-based armed conflicts worldwide from 1946 to 2025, rising to a record 65 in 2025, with a second line showing conflicts between states reaching 8 in 2025, also the highest since 1946.
feature_images.caption: Active armed conflicts reached 65 in 2025, a record since 1946. Eight were state against state, the kind that moves oil, shipping and insurance.
feature_images.source: Source: UCDP/PRIO Armed Conflict Dataset via Our World in Data; 2025 figures confirmed by Uppsala University, June 9, 2026.
